items.name: Dazaifu Tenmangu
items.kicker: Shrine of scholarship, over Michizane's grave
items.body: Built over the grave of Sugawara no Michizane, deified as Tenjin — the head shrine of roughly 12,000 Tenjin shrines nationwide, and a pilgrimage site for students praying over exams. Free to enter; the small Treasure Hall and history museum are optional paid add-ons. Arrive near opening to beat the tour-bus crowds.

items.name: Kyushu National Museum
items.kicker: Japan's cultural exchange with Asia, next door to the shrine
items.body: One of Japan's four national museums, focused on Japan's historical exchange with the rest of Asia. ¥700 for the regular collection; no special exhibition runs during this trip's exact dates. Closed Mondays.

items.name: Fukuoka Castle Ruins (Maizuru Park)
items.kicker: Free stone-wall ruins in a central city park
items.body: The stone foundations and walls of Fukuoka's Edo-period castle, free to walk year-round. The park's famous for cherry blossoms in spring, which this October trip won't see — the ruins themselves are the draw regardless of season.

items.name: Ohori Park
items.kicker: A ~2km pond loop next to the castle ruins
items.body: A large central pond ringed by a walking/jogging path, opened in 1927 on a former Hakata Bay inlet. Free, always open, and an easy pairing with the adjacent castle ruins for a morning walk.

items.name: Kushida Shrine
items.kicker: Hakata's guardian shrine, with a year-round festival float
items.body: Founded 757 CE, home to a 1,000-plus-year-old ginkgo tree and a ≈13m ornamental Hakata Gion Yamakasa float on year-round display (except June). Free to enter; on Oct 23–24 the shrine hosts Hakata Okunchi, a free harvest festival.

items.name: Sakurai Futamigaura
items.kicker: A shrine torii gate standing in the ocean
items.body: Itoshima's signature photo spot — two "husband and wife" rocks joined by a sacred rope ≈150m offshore, with a torii gate in the water. Free, best at sunset. Public buses run infrequently; a taxi or car is the practical way in. The sunset view draws real crowds and a parking lot that fills fast, especially around the summer solstice and weekend/holiday evenings — arrive at least an hour early, or visit midday/on a weekday to skip the worst of it.

items.name: Shiraito Falls
items.kicker: A 24m waterfall with trout for lunch
items.body: A free waterfall on Mt. Hagane, with an on-site restaurant (Shiki no Chaya) serving yamame mountain-trout set meals and hand-pulled soba — a genuine regional specialty. Bus access is a sparse connection plus a ≈30-minute walk; a taxi or car is more realistic for a group.

items.name: Nokonoshima Island Park
items.kicker: A flower park reached by a short city ferry
items.body: An island flower park a 10-minute municipal ferry ride from Meinohama (¥230 each way), with cosmos flowers typically in bloom in this exact window — though the 2026 bloom timing itself isn't published this far ahead. Open year-round, no closed days.

items.claim: Dazaifu Tenmangu's big autumn festival makes late September through October a can't-miss window.
items.correction: The shrine's major annual festival, Jinkosai, runs Sept 21–25 — a full month before this trip. Visiting Oct 19–23 means missing both the festival and its crowds; the shrine's daily quiet-hour advice (near opening) matters more than any festival timing for this trip.

items.claim: Kushida Shrine's Hakata Gion Yamakasa float is a special, paid attraction.
items.correction: The ornamental float is on free, year-round display as part of the shrine grounds (except during June) — no separate ticket. Paid seating only applies to the live Yamakasa event itself, which runs in July, not this trip.

items.claim: A group can just walk into a yatai stall together for dinner.
items.correction: Fukuoka's own tourism board recommends parties of 2–3 at a yatai and warns larger groups may be turned away outright — stalls seat roughly 8–10 total, including everyone else already there. An 8-person group needs to split up, not queue together.

items.claim: Komyozenji, the moss-garden temple next to Dazaifu Tenmangu, is a reliable quiet alternative worth building the day around.
items.correction: It's genuinely calmer than the shrine whenever it's open — but a maintained English-language travel reference describes it as not regularly open to the public, and several visitors independently report finding the gate closed on arrival. Treat it as a zero-commitment "check on arrival" peek, not a planned stop.
